title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
authors: Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, Yoshua Bengio

pages.title: The big idea
pages.subtitle: Let the decoder look back at the whole source

blocks.html: Seq2seq translation squeezes an entire source sentence into a single fixed-length vector and asks the decoder to reconstruct the translation from it. This paper makes one sharp diagnosis: that fixed-length vector is a bottleneck. The longer the sentence, the more the model must cram into the same number of slots, and quality on long sentences collapses.

The fix is the mechanism we now call attention. Instead of forcing one summary vector to carry everything, keep all of the encoder's per-word representations around. As the decoder produces each target word, it builds a fresh context vector — a weighted blend of the source representations — focusing on whichever source words are most relevant right now.
The model learns to (soft-)align and translate jointly: it figures out which source words to attend to at the same time as it figures out how to translate them, with no alignment supervision at all.

The result matched a strong phrase-based system on English-French, and the gains were concentrated exactly where the old model failed — on long sentences. This soft-alignment idea is the direct ancestor of the attention in the Transformer.

pages.title: The fixed-vector bottleneck
pages.subtitle: Why one summary vector isn't enough

blocks.html: In the original encoder-decoder, the encoder reads the source and hands the decoder a single vector $c$ — its last hidden state. Everything the decoder ever knows about the source must pass through that one vector. For a short sentence that is fine. For a thirty- or fifty-word sentence, it is a severe compression.

The authors point to the empirical symptom: the basic encoder-decoder's performance degrades rapidly as sentences grow longer. It is being asked to remember too much in too little space, and the early parts of long sentences get crushed.

The conceptual move is to stop summarizing prematurely. A human translator does not read the whole sentence, memorize a single impression, and then translate from memory with the source hidden. They glance back at the relevant words as they write. The model should be allowed to do the same.

pages.title: A bidirectional encoder of annotations
pages.subtitle: One vector per source word, not one per sentence

blocks.html: The encoder is a bidirectional RNN. A forward RNN reads the sentence left to right, a backward RNN reads it right to left, and for each source position $j$ their two hidden states are concatenated into an annotation $h_j$.

Each annotation $h_j$ summarizes the whole sentence but with a strong focus on the words around position $j$, because the recurrent state nearest a word reflects it most. So instead of one vector for the sentence, the encoder produces a sequence of annotations $(h_1,\\dots,h_{T_x})$ — roughly one rich vector per source word — and all of them are kept for the decoder to consult.

pages.title: The attention mechanism, step by step
pages.subtitle: Score, normalize, blend

blocks.html: Here is the heart of the paper. When the decoder is about to emit target word $i$, it does three things. First it scores how well each source annotation $h_j$ matches its current need, using its previous hidden state $s_{i-1}$:

Read this as: an alignment score $e_{ij}$ measuring how relevant source word $j$ is to producing target word $i$. The scorer $a$ is a small feed-forward network trained jointly with everything else — there is no separate alignment step and no alignment labels.
Second, it turns those raw scores into weights that sum to one, via a softmax over all source positions:
Read this as: the attention weight $\\alpha_{ij}$ is the fraction of attention target word $i$ pays to source word $j$. A weight near 1 means ‘this source word is what I care about right now.’
Third, it forms the context vector as the weighted sum of the annotations:

Read this as: a custom summary $c_i$ built fresh for target word $i$, mostly made of the source words it is attending to. Crucially $c_i$ changes at every output step — the decoder gets a different view of the source for every word it writes.

pages.title: Decoding with a moving context
pages.subtitle: Each output word gets its own view of the source

blocks.html: The decoder is still a recurrent network, but its state and its output now depend on the step-specific context $c_i$ instead of one global vector. The probability of each target word is:

where the decoder state is updated as $s_i = f(s_{i-1},\\, y_{i-1},\\, c_i)$. In words: to choose the next word, look at the previous word, the decoder's running state, and the freshly computed context that points at the relevant source words.

Because the whole pipeline — scorer, softmax, weighted sum — is differentiable, the network learns where to look purely from the pressure to translate well. This is ‘soft’ alignment: rather than committing to one source word, the model spreads a probability distribution over all of them, which is what makes it trainable by gradient descent.

pages.title: Big gains on long sentences
pages.subtitle: Exactly where the bottleneck used to bite

blocks.html: On WMT'14 English-French, the attention model (RNNsearch) clearly beat the plain encoder-decoder (RNNenc), and the new model with attention matched a conventional phrase-based system — remarkable for a pure neural model in 2015.

The most telling plot is BLEU versus sentence length. The plain encoder-decoder's quality falls off a cliff as sentences get longer, while the attention model stays roughly flat well past fifty words. That is direct confirmation that the fixed-vector bottleneck was the culprit, and that letting the decoder look back removes it.

pages.title: Attention as interpretable alignment
pages.subtitle: The weights line up with human intuition

blocks.html: Because the attention weights $\\alpha_{ij}$ form a matrix over source and target positions, you can simply plot them. The result is a soft alignment map showing which source words each output word drew from.

These maps agree with human intuition: mostly a near-diagonal monotonic alignment, but with sensible reorderings — for example handling adjective-noun order differences between English and French — that a rigid left-to-right model could never express. The model learned to reorder when the languages demand it, all without alignment labels.
This interpretability was a bonus that made attention enormously popular: you can see what the model is doing.

The score-softmax-blend pattern introduced here is the conceptual core of all modern attention. Three years later, ‘Attention Is All You Need’ threw away the recurrent backbone entirely and kept only this mechanism, generalized into self-attention and stacked into the Transformer.

Read with hindsight, this paper is the hinge between the RNN era and the Transformer era: it found the one piece of the encoder-decoder that was doing the heavy lifting, gave it a clean differentiable form, and showed it could be learned end to end. Everything from GPT to BERT inherits the idea that a model should learn, for each output, what to pay attention to.
